questions.def: "So" modifies an adjective (difficult) to show degree.
questions.question: The task was ___ difficult that few completed it.

questions.def: "Such" modifies a noun phrase (a compelling argument).
questions.question: It was ___ a compelling argument that everyone agreed.

questions.def: "Enough" follows the adjective it modifies.
questions.question: The findings were ___ to warrant further study.

questions.def: "Enough" comes after the adjective it modifies.
questions.question: He wasn't experienced ___ to handle the project alone.

questions.def: "So" is used with "as to" to show result.
questions.question: The evidence was ___ compelling as to be undeniable.

questions.def: An adjective is needed to modify "enough".
questions.question: The argument wasn't ___ enough to sway the jury.

questions.def: "So" is used before "many/few/much/little".
questions.question: The report contained ___ many errors that it was rejected.

questions.def: "So" is used before "little" to indicate degree.
questions.question: There was ___ little evidence to support the claim.

questions.def: "Too" requires an adjective and "to" + infinitive.
questions.question: The lecture was ___ to sit through.

questions.def: "Such" modifies a noun phrase (a great understanding).
questions.question: She has ___ a great understanding of the subject.

questions.def: "So" is used in negative comparisons with "as".
questions.question: The problem is not ___ difficult as it seems.

questions.def: "So" modifies an adjective and implies a consequence.
questions.question: The book was ___ interesting that I read it twice.

questions.def: "So" modifies an adjective (small) to show degree.
questions.question: The room was ___ small that it felt claustrophobic.

questions.def: "Such" modifies a noun phrase (a beautiful day).
questions.question: It was ___ a beautiful day that we went for a walk.

questions.def: "Enough" follows the adjective or comes before the noun.
questions.question: She didn't have ___ experience to qualify.

questions.def: "Too" means more than is desirable or acceptable.
questions.question: He was ___ tired to concentrate on the task.

questions.def: "Too" implies a negative consequence or limitation.
questions.question: The question was ___ difficult for them to answer.

questions.def: Should be "such" before much + noun (money).
questions.question: He has so much money that he doesn't know what to do.

questions.def: An adjective is needed to modify "enough".
questions.question: The team was ___ enough to win the championship.

questions.def: "Such" modifies a noun phrase (a masterpiece).
questions.question: The novel was ___ a masterpiece that it won several awards.

questions.def: "So" precedes adjective when followed by "as to".
questions.question: She is ___ an intelligent student as to grasp the concepts quickly.

questions.def: "Too" before an adjective implies difficulty/impossibility.
questions.question: The report was ___ detailed to be summarized easily.

questions.def: "So" modifies an adjective (unclear) to indicate degree.
questions.question: The instructions were ___ unclear that nobody understood them.

questions.def: "So" is used before "little" to emphasize scarcity.
questions.question: There is ___ little time left to complete the project.

questions.def: "Enough" follows the adjective: tall enough.
questions.question: The building was enough tall to be seen from miles away.

questions.def: "Too" indicates an excessive degree leading to a negative result.
questions.question: He is ___ skilled to need assistance.

questions.def: "So" is used with "as to" to express a result.
questions.question: The music was ___ loud as to be unbearable.

questions.def: "So much" precedes uncountable nouns.
questions.question: The proposal lacked ___ detail as to be approved.

questions.def: Use "so" before "many", not "such".
questions.question: The task required such many resources that it proved difficult.

questions.def: "So" modifies an adjective; "compelling" is an adjective.
questions.question: The evidence was ___ compelling that a conviction was inevitable.
